newsitem.title: UK: Dollar subdued in Europe, sterling eyes UK rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar subdued in Europe, sterling eyes UK rates.

text.p: The dollar was steady but subdued in early trading as traders eyed a slew of German economic data and awaited the outcome of today's UK monthly monetary meeting, unexpectedly brought forward from Wednesday.

The dollar retreated from overnight highs against the mark and the yen amid some fresh optimism about economic activity in Germany and Japan but traders said there was little net change in the U.S. unit from Monday's levels.
"The dollar's pretty flat from yesterday close and looks well supported around current levels," said Ian Gunner, economist at Chase Investment Bank.

At 0820 GMT, the dollar was trading 1.7281/86 marks compared with 1.7283/88 late Monday. A bank holiday on Monday in London, Europe's biggest foreign exchange trading centre, kept trading volumes to a minimum yesterday, traders said.

Details of the April German unemployment report leaked out on Monday and proved broadly in line with the official data released early Tuesday. Seasonally-adjusted jobless rose 8,000 during the month, with a drop in the unadjusted unemployment rate to 11.3 percent from 11.7 percent in March.
Earlier, the April German Purchasing Managers Index reinforced a view of a recovering German economy.
The German PMI rose to 56.58 from 54.58 in March.

Despite the rise in German economic activity, jitters about an interest rate rise in Japan are more pronounced and the yen gained against both the dollar and mark overnight while Japanese government bond yields pushed higher.

The higher sensitivity of the yen to rate rise talk is partly because cheap yen borrowings have been used by investors around the world over the past year to fund high-yield holdings. Any prospect of a change in the cost of yen borrowing prompts profit taking on these positions, analysts said.
European monetary union remains a weight on the mark.

The rigours of the EMU timetable mean there is a greater need for tight fiscal than tight monetary policy in Germany and around Europe and, therefore, less of a chance of higher interest rates there in the medium-term.

"There seems to be a consensus building that G3 rate rises will be staggered and quite far apart - the U.S. has already moved, the pressure in Japan is building and continental Europe will lag for some time," said a senior trader at a U.S. bank here. "Mark/yen is very vulnerable in that set up."
At 0850 GMT, the mark/yen cross was at 72.75/77 compared with 73.17/20 late Monday.
The main focus for many London traders, meantime, was the surprise announcement that the monthly UK monetary meeting had been brought forward from Wednesday to today.

The meeting is the first between new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown and Bank of England governor Eddie George since the Labour Party victory in last week's UK election. Brown is scheduled to make a statement at 1000 GMT.

"It looks like we're going to get a quarter-point rate rise," said Gunner at Chase. "The change in timing suggests Brown is keen to make a forceful move and take the initiative This should be good for the markets and positive for sterling."

The pound, which had been well off overnight highs against the mark, firmed initially back above 2.80 marks on the news of today's meeting but has slipped back since as the 1000 GMT announment is awaited.
